title: Route 66 Turns 100: A Brewery-by-Brewery Road Trip Guide From Chicago to Santa Monica
summary:
Starting in Chicago, running through Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona, and ending in Santa Monica, Calif., Route 66 was established in 1926. Although Route 66 was officially removed from the United States Highway System in 1985, it remains in the national consciousness with cities along the route using it to promote tourism to this day. With 2026 marking Route 66’s centennial, many towns are promoting nostalgia in their tourism advertising.

content:
Starting in Chicago, running through Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona, and ending in Santa Monica, Calif., Route 66 was established in 1926. Although Route 66 was officially removed from the United States Highway System in 1985, it remains in the national consciousness with cities along the route using it to promote tourism to this day.

With 2026 marking Route 66’s centennial, many towns are promoting nostalgia in their tourism advertising. The Mother Road — as Route 66 came to be known after John Steinbeck dubbed it so in his book “The Grapes of Wrath” — was designed to pass through small towns to boost their local economies. It’s a road trip through time and its 100th anniversary is a great reason to take to the highway.

While Nov. 11 is the official date Route 66 was established, the summer driving season is the perfect opportunity to explore the famed highway and celebrate its centennial. The U.S. is now home to over 9,000 breweries. Arguably, America is the home of the modern craft beer movement. Every major city and many small towns now have breweries, many of which only offer their beer on site. Route 66 makes its way through many of these towns, so it’s a great way to try beers that aren’t available anywhere else.

Pack your bags, grab your designated driver, and hit up these 66 breweries along Route 66.

Chicago

Chicago is a great town for drinks and there are many amazing breweries in the Windy City. But the “Begin Route 66” sign in Chicago is on E. Adams Street near Michigan Avenue, near the Art Institute of Chicago and the iconic Cloud Gate sculpture, better known as “the Bean.” The nearest brewery is Industry Ales Brewpub — a spot VinePair listed as one of the best new breweries of 2024 — just around the corner from the sign, on S. Wabash Ave. On Route 66 itself, just a block west of the sign is an outlet of the Adam Street Brewery, located in the Berghoff Restaurant, which has been family-owned and -operated for more than a century.

The Rest of Illinois

Leaving Chicago, Route 66 heads southwest. As the highway nears Lyons, BuckleDown Brewing is just a short deviation off the path. Farther along, Route 66 passes through Willowbrook, where beer lovers can visit Black Horizon Brewing Company for a taproom experience that not only features beer, but also pinball and classic arcade games. And as Route 66 passes through Plainfield, there are two potential stops: Werk Force Brewing — which boasts an astounding 29 taps — and Garage Band Brewing.

The Gemini Giant is a 30-foot-tall fiberglass sculpture in Wilmington. It is the perfect stop for a photograph. And not far away is the appropriately named RT66 Old School Brewing, a family-owned spot that even features a specialty brew to celebrate the highway: the RT66 Haze. Continuing south, Route 66 then passes through Lexington, home to Analytical Brewing, which also has a location in Peoria.

The next major stop is Bloomington. DESTIHL Brewery is directly on Route 66 in Normal, the town just north of Bloomington and is worth a stop before heading into Bloomington proper. DESTIHL is the largest brewery in the area with beer so well regarded, it has been distributed internationally. Fiala Brothers Brewery, White Oak Brewing, and Lil Beaver Brewery all call Bloomington home, though none are directly on Route 66.

Leaving Bloomington, Route 66 goes southwest through Atlanta, Ill., where Midway 154 Brewing will begin serving its own beers on site in 2026. This is a good stop, as is Limerick Brewing located within Spirited Republic in Lincoln, a bar featuring 40 taps, including brews from other local spots as well.

Route 66 passed through three different routes in Springfield, Ill., thanks to periodic rererouting of the highway. Whichever route you choose to take, Obed & Isaac’s Microbrewery, Bald Buddha Brewing, Engrained Brewing Company, and Springfield Beer Company are nearby. Both Obed & Issac’s and Engrained offer full food menus, so they make good stops for meals as well as beer. And just south of Springfield, in Chatham, Sangamo Brewing is yet another beer destination on the Mother Road.

Just before Route 66 exits Illinois, Mississippi Culture is a worthy stop in Staunton that frequently features live music, if you want to coordinate your visit with a show.

St. Louis

St. Louis and its greater metropolitan area are home to over 70 breweries, including its most famous, Anheuser-Busch. Despite working in the shadow of the world’s largest brewing company, the craft beer scene has thrived in St. Louis.

Since the path of Route 66 through the Gateway to the West changed a few times, there are a number of breweries on or near one of the official Route 66 paths: Urban Chestnut Brewing, Schlafly Bottleworks, Heavy Riff Brewing, and Side Project Brewing all qualify as stops on this ultimate Route 66 brewery tour. Schlafly, which started operations in 1991, is notable as the first new brewery in St. Louis to open since Prohibition.

The Rest of Missouri

As Route 66 heads west leaving St. Louis, Point Labaddie Brewery is in Labadie — yes, the brewery and the town are spelled differently. Point Labaddie is located on a large parcel of land so it can host live music and farmers markets.

As the Mother Road enters Sullivan, veteran-owned and -operated Muddy Banks Brewing is directly on the route. And as Route 66 continues farther west through St. James, it passes by Public House Brewing, which also has a location in Rolla. In Waynesville, the Piney River Taproom is directly on the historic highway. And Boat Town Brewing is a good stop for barrel-aged brews in Lebanon, Mo.

The second Springfield on Route 66, this one in Missouri, is home to a number of breweries. On or near the route are Hold Fast Brewing, Springfield Brewing Company, and Mother’s Brewing Company. Springfield Brewing also has an onsite distillery that has made commemorative Route 66 spirits.

Kansas

Only 13 miles of Route 66 pass through Kansas and no breweries are directly on the route. The brewery within Kansas closest to Route 66 is Drop the H Brewing — which also offers some destination-worthy homemade pizzas — in Pittsburg, Kan., a short detour north.

Tulsa

Over 400 miles of Route 66 go through the Sooner State, more than any other state. As Route 66 heads southwest through Oklahoma, the first breweries are in Tulsa, home to the Route 66 Historic Village tourist destination.

As Route 66 heads west along 11th Street in Tulsa, it passes just a few blocks south of Marshall Brewing, Cabin Boys Brewery, and Nothing’s Left Brewing. While each of these breweries is worthy of a stop, Nothing’s Left is located in a former Texaco station, giving it an extra nostalgic appeal appropriate for this Route 66 tour.

The Rest of Oklahoma

James Calley Brewing is just one block north of Route 66 as it passes through Sapulpa. And for those wanting to dial up the nostalgia, nearby is the Heart of Route 66 Auto Museum. As Route 66 junctions with the Northwest Expressway in Oklahoma City, just off the highway is Belle Isle Restaurant & Pub, a full-service restaurant and brewery with a live music venue upstairs. Further into Oklahoma City, Okie Beer Co. features a broad selection of beers from clean and light lagers to rich and heavy imperial stouts.

Texas

Route 66 crosses the northernmost area of Texas. The most major city along the route is Amarillo — there is a variety of hop named “Amarillo.” The Yellow Rose of Texas is home to several breweries, but the two closest to Route 66 are Six Car Pub & Brewery and Old Tascosa Brewery, the latter of which offers a special Route 66 witbier called Wit 66.

Eastern New Mexico

Route 66 passes south of Sante Fe, so the first brewery stop in New Mexico is not until Moriarty, where Sierra Blanca Brewing offers a lively outdoor beer garden. Despite having a population of just over 2,000 people, Moriarty actually boasts two breweries, and Turquoise Trail Brewing is the next stop on the Mother Road brewery trip. Both breweries are directly on Route 66, just south of I-40.

Albuquerque

Fun fact: Route 66 actually intersects itself in Albuquerque. Originally, the highway ran north-south along Fourth Street. In 1937, the highway was rerouted to run east-west along Central Avenue, creating the interesting intersection.

But before reaching Fourth Street, Central Avenue passes just one block north of Bombs Away Beer. Continuing west, Route 66 then passes by Flock of Moons Brewing and then one block north of Thirsty Eye Brewing, which offers not only beer, but also curated exhibits from local artists. On Second Street, Sidetrack Brewing is three blocks south of Route 66, while Ex Novo Brewing is the next brewery stop directly on the route.

The historic El Vado Motel was one of New Mexico’s first motels on Route 66 and today is also home to El Vado Taproom, which is an outlet of Ponderosa Brewing. There’s perhaps no better place to lay your head down to sleep than this iconic motel.

As Route 66 exits Albuquerque, it passes just south of Unhinged Brewing & Distilling where handcrafted artisan pizza satisfies the appetite before hitting the highway again.

The Rest of New Mexico

In western New Mexico, Route 66 passes through Grants. Junkyard on 66 Brewery is directly on the route, while Elkins Brewing is just a short detour south. Bonus: Junkyard on 66 Brewery is a Harvest Hosts RV site.

Arizona

Through Arizona, Route 66 passes directly through Flagstaff. There, beer lovers can stop at Wanderlust Brewing and the appropriately named Mother Road Brewing. For a break from beer, Mother Road also offers an evening cocktail bar named Jimmy D’s Five Spot.

The next Arizona stop along Route 66 is Williams. There, Historic Brewing Barrel House is home to a location of Flagstaff’s Historic Brewing. Here, 16 beers are available to accompany a full menu of pizzas and sandwiches.

Finally, in Kingman, Route 66 passes by Rickety Cricket Brewing, Black Bridge Brewery, and the Kingman location of Williams’ Grand Canyon Brewing + Distillery. Grand Canyon, as its name implies, has a distillery, so it offers not only beer, but also spirits and pre-mixed cocktails.

For those interested, Arizona also boasts a sake brewery on Route 66, Arizona Sake in Holbrook, before Route 66 reaches Flagstaff.

California

The first California stop on the Route 66 brewery tour is the Victorville location of BJ’s Restaurant & Brewhouse. Founded in 1996, BJ’s has over 200 locations across America and no cross-country road trip would be complete without stopping at a minimum of one BJ’s location.

Route 66 then passes through Upland. Mt Baldy Brewery is just north of Route 66 while Dragon’s Tale Brewery is just south. For chocolate lovers, Dragon’s Tale offers handmade chocolates infused with bourbon or beer.

In Arcadia, Route 66 passes by another location of BJ’s Brewhouse, and just south of Mt. Lowe Brewing in Pasadena, Route 66 passes by Wild Parrot Brewing. The Mother Road then turns south and passes by the Pasadena location of the legendary Stone Brewing.

As Route 66 follows Sunset Boulevard in Los Angeles, it passes by the Echo Park location of Monkish Brewing Co., known best for its Belgian-inspired brews, though it offers a full suite of beers in a broad array of styles.

Santa Monica Brew Works is just two blocks south of Route 66 and is the last brewery stop before Route 66 ends at the intersection of Lincoln Boulevard and Olympic Boulevard, as marked by a sign that says “End of the Trail.”

Modern highways are designed to get people to their destinations quickly. But Route 66 meanders, designed to promote the economies of the cities and towns along its route. This is why it captured the American consciousness and was immortalized in popular culture. Route 66 has always been the ultimate road trip and its centennial is the perfect reason to enjoy almost 2,500 miles of Americana.

title: Scotland’s Scotch Whisky Regions, Mapped
summary:
In the grand scope of whisky, Scotch is a universe unto itself. Across malt, grain, and blended whisky producers, Scotland is home to some of the most iconic brands in the world, along with an incredibly high density of distilleries. The Scotch Whisky Association (SWA) — the trade body representing the vast majority of Scotch whisky production — counts 154 malt and grain distilleries as of 2026. That list boasts incredible diversity across styles, flavors, and production techniques. Yet one of the most common ways to parse Scotch distilleries is by region.

content:
In the grand scope of whisky, Scotch is a universe unto itself. Across malt, grain, and blended whisky producers, Scotland is home to some of the most iconic brands in the world, along with an incredibly high density of distilleries. The Scotch Whisky Association (SWA) — the trade body representing the vast majority of Scotch whisky production — counts 154 malt and grain distilleries as of 2026. That list boasts incredible diversity across styles, flavors, and production techniques.

Yet one of the most common ways to parse Scotch distilleries is by region. The partitioning of Scotch into distinct areas traces its early origins to the Wash Act of 1784, which drew an imaginary line dividing the Highland and Lowland regions. This created differing legal and tax requirements for production, including still size and speed. The Act’s implications influenced production methods and helped spur the development of individual styles.

As laws changed and the industry grew, other regional designations gradually developed, often more geographical than stylistic. By 1909, the U.K.’s Royal Commission on Whisky and Other Potable Spirits included the five Scotch whisky regions still widely recognized today: Highlands, Lowlands, Speyside, Islay, and Campbeltown. In 2009, The Scotch Whisky Regulations formally acknowledged three protected regions (“Highland,” “Lowland,” and “Speyside”) along with two protected localities (“Islay” and “Campbeltown”).

Today, those five areas comprise the official Scotch geographic designations. Each features a diverse array of whisky styles, and the modern regions often speak more to history and proximity than flavor profile. A sixth, informal designation — the Islands — has emerged due to the proliferation of new distilleries across the Inner and Outer Hebrides, in addition to the Northern Isles. Though technically still a part of the Highlands, for the purposes of this article and graphic, we’re breaking out the Islands into its own classification. Read on to discover more about each of these regions — and the range of whiskies to expect from each.

The Highlands

The Highlands are separated from the Lowlands by an imaginary line slicing across Scotland, from Dundee in the east to Greenock in the west. That artificial divide can lead to some categorical oddities. For example, Glengoyne is a Highland single malt producer that straddles the border. Its stills are situated in the Highlands, while its warehouses — nestled across a single road — are in the Lowlands region.

By far the largest Scotch region, the Highlands traditionally includes most of the country’s surrounding islands, with the notable exception of Islay. Its distilleries are situated over an array of terrain, climates, and water sources.

Accordingly, the region’s whisky exists across a wide spectrum of styles, one that’s difficult to bucket into a particular flavor profile. Highlands whiskies range from full-bodied, heavily sherried Glendronach bottlings to Glenmorangie, which utilizes the country’s tallest pot stills for a lighter and more floral spirit. The region is sometimes (and unofficially) subdivided into the Northern, Southern, Western, Eastern, and/or Central Highlands.

Speyside

Speyside is located in the northeastern Highlands, with distilleries concentrated along the River Spey, which historically provided ample freshwater for whisky production. While technically a subregion, Speyside’s unique history and styles have led to separate recognition and special status. Contemporary Speyside distilleries can choose whether to market their whiskies as either Highland or Speyside. For example, the Macallan labels its bottles as Highland single malts while frequently emphasizing its Speyside heritage. (“Nestled Above the River Spey” is a common refrain in its marketing.)

Speyside currently has more than 50 active distilleries, more than any other Scotch region; the SWA calls Speyside “the most densely populated whisky region in the world.” Speyside whiskies are celebrated for sweet, fruit-forward profiles, and distillers commonly mature across ex-bourbon and/or sherry casks. (The latter style often leads to more robust flavors, richer in dark fruits.) Large and prominent producers include Glenfiddich, Glenlivet, and Roseisle, to name a few. While Speyside whiskies are best known for being unpeated, some distilleries — including Balvenie, Benriach, and Benromach — also produce peated distillate.

The Lowlands

Scotland’s Lowland whiskies span a range of styles. In addition to single malts, the area is famed for its grain whisky distilleries, which typically employ high-volume distillation via column (or “continuous”) stills. It’s home to large-scale operations like Cameronbridge, widely recognized as Europe’s highest-volume grain distillery. Historically, Lowland grain whiskies have been integral components of blended Scotch, though some are commonly released and branded under various single grain labels.

The Lowlands is also home to a number of well-regarded single malt producers, including Auchentoshan, Bladnoch, Glenkinchie, Daftmill, and Rosebank, which was shuttered for decades before restarting production in 2023. Lowland single malts are known for showcasing lighter flavors, in addition to both floral and grassy profiles. In recent years, the style has expanded as producers experiment with and incorporate various techniques, including peated whiskies.

Campbeltown

The smallest of Scotland’s whisky regions, Campbeltown is located on the Kintyre Peninsula in western Scotland’s Argyll and Bute, a unitary council area. In the late 1800s, Campbeltown was home to roughly 30 distilleries. That extreme density of production led to its moniker as “Whisky Capital of the World.” Today, those numbers have dwindled to just three operating distilleries: Springbank, Glen Scotia, and Glengyle.

While no longer in its powerhouse heyday, Campbeltown is still an influential locale for distilling, producing a wide variety of flavors. The three current Campbeltown producers are known for a breadth of whisky styles, even within the same distillery: peated and unpeated malts, heavy and lighter distillates, and a mix of ex-bourbon and sherry cask maturation. Many Campbeltown expressions are renowned for an oily texture and sea-influenced briny flavors.

Islay

The only Scottish island with an approved SWA designation, Islay lies to the west of the mainland and is the southernmost of the Inner Hebrides. With a permanent population of around 3,000 inhabitants, Islay is home to 11 modern distilleries: Ardbeg, Lagavulin, Laphroaig, Port Ellen, Caol Ila, Bunnahabhain, Ardnahoe, Bowmore, Bruichladdich, Kilchoman, and Laggan Bay. Alongside farming, whisky is one of the island’s main economic drivers and largest employment sectors.

Islay distilleries are famed for producing some of the world’s most heavily peated single malts, with pronounced smoky flavors ranging from meaty to medicinal. However, not all Islay whisky is peated. Bunnahabhain’s core offerings are unpeated, and its limited peated offerings tend to showcase a lighter side of smoke. Bruichladdich also produces a range of whiskies across the smoky spectrum, ranging from unpeated (the flagship Bruichladdich line) to the “super heavily peated” Octomore series.

The Islands

Under Scottish law, there is no official “Islands” category for Scotch. The term generally refers to whiskies produced across the islands of Arran, Jura, Mull, Orkney, Skye, Lewis, Harris, Raasay, and Shetland — all of which technically fall within the Highlands.

In recent decades, the islands have seen a proliferation of distilleries. Founded in 2017, Torabhaig was the first new legal distillery on Skye in almost 190 years, joining Talisker (founded in 1830) in producing peaty, briny malts. Founded in 2015 and 2017, respectively, the Isle of Harris and Isle of Raasay distilleries became the first legal spirits producers on their islands. The informal Islands region also encompasses Scotland’s northernmost distilleries, including Highland Park and Scapa (Orkney). Lerwick Distillery, located on the Shetland Islands more than 100 miles north of the Scottish mainland, is currently aging casks for its first release.

The region’s styles vary, though whisky makers frequently take advantage of extreme climates, allowing coastal winds and sea spray to batter warehouses as spirits age.

*Image retrieved from Rick Barrett for Ambitious Studio via unsplash.com

content:
When the warm weather hits right, a chilled glass of rosé is hard to beat. But we’re not talking about just “any” rosé. We’re uncorking one from Provence.

Provence isn’t just famous for rosé. It’s the only major wine region on Earth entirely dedicated to it. Across three protected appellations d’origine contrôlée (AOPs) stretching 200 kilometers from the foothills of the Alps to the Mediterranean coast, 5,000 growers have spent decades perfecting a single style: pale, precise, and instantly recognizable anywhere in the world.

That style is built on a mosaic of soils, microclimates, and grape varieties that no other region can replicate. Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah, Mourvèdre, and Rolle — always blended and balanced — produce wines that range from delicate and floral to rich and mineral, giving drinkers a genuine diversity of expression under one unmistakable identity. 

Its signature color, ranging from pale salmon to faint blush, is intentional. Short maceration, often through direct press, extracts just enough pigment for aromatic depth without adding heavy tannins. Older vintages that have spent more time in the barrel can develop richer, spiced, ripe-fruit profiles.

The other main ingredient is terroir. Provence averages around 3,000 hours of sunshine and just 2.5 inches of rain per year, stressing the vines enough to concentrate flavor while delivering a rich ripeness of the fruit without excess alcohol. 

Soils range from crystalline schist (granite) and limestone to clay and coastal sandy soils, giving each wine a distinct personality. And cutting through it all, the Mistral, a cold, dry wind that sweeps the landscape regularly, keeps the grapes dry, reduces disease pressure, and preserves the crisp acidity that’s come to define every great Provençal rosé.

The region also has some of the wine world’s most rigorous sustainability commitments: 67 percent of vineyards are organic or HVE certified, 82 percent are cover-cropped, and every bottle carries the PDO designation, Europe’s most demanding quality guarantee.

At the table, Provence rosé earns its keep. Its crisp acidity, subtle fruit, and dry finish make it one of the most food-versatile wines. Equally a perfect option for sushi, barbecue ribs, spiced Indian dishes, or a cheeseburger with aioli.

From vine to cellar to bottle, every stage is meticulous for rosé: selecting the best grapes, nighttime harvesting to preserve aromatics, continuous temperature control, and vinification by direct press or cold skin maceration. 

Here are some quick facts to deepen your ​​savoir-rosé.

title: Booze News Weekly Roundup: Brown-Forman Turns Down Another Sazerac Offer, U.S. Lifts Tariffs from Scotch Whisky, and More
summary:
This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have news on Sazerac’s request from Brown-Forman to reconsider its previous offer, a co-signed letter lobbying for alcohol health warning labels on bottles, the latest product releases, and more. News to know: Sazerac tried to court Brown-Forman yet again.

content:
This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have news on Sazerac’s request from Brown-Forman to reconsider its previous offer, a co-signed letter lobbying for alcohol health warning labels on bottles, the latest product releases, and more.

News to know:

  • Sazerac tried to court Brown-Forman yet again. Sazerac, which owns brands like BuzzBallz and Buffalo Trace, sent a letter to the maker of Jack Daniel’s and Woodford Reserve earlier this week, asking to reconsider its original $15 billion buyout offer. Brown-Forman later issued a statement denying the reconsideration. Sazerac first approached Brown-Forman about an acquisition back in April a few days after reports revealed the American whiskey juggernaut had engaged in potential deal talks with Pernod Ricard.
  • A coalition of trade groups co-signed a public statement addressed to Department of Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., and Treasury secretary Scott Bessent lobbying for a legislation that would require alcohol companies to brandish their products with a warning label about their health effects. The trade groups ask for the administration officials’ support to “help fulfill President Trump’s goal of Making America Healthy Again.”
  • Last dance for the Margarita? Data from NielsenIQ shows the Martini is nipping at the heels of the Margarita, the most-purchased cocktail in the U.S. In the final fiscal quarter of 2025, on-premise accounts in the U.S. saw a 16 percent drop in revenue from Margarita purchases year-over-year. Martinis, however, brought those accounts 29 percent more in revenue than the year prior. While the Margarita remains the prima donna of cocktails, the Martini’s time at the top could be on the horizon.
  • President Donald Trump’s lift on Scotch whisky tariffs came into effect on Friday. Trump and Scotland came to a zero-for-zero trade deal during King Charles’ visit to the U.S. in April. The lift means American whiskey will also enter the U.K. without the added taxes.
  • Famed Sonoma winemaking pioneer David Hirsch passed away at 81. Hirsch was one of the earliest influential viticulturists in the region: His work on his vineyard site on the extreme Sonoma Coast in the 1980s and ’90s drew flocks of aspiring winemakers to Sonoma, an exodus that helped establish the region as among the best in the world.

Product releases to watch:

  • Middle West Spirits-owned Old Elk Distillery released a trio of 10-year-old whiskeys, including a straight bourbon, wheat whiskey, and wheated bourbon. The bourbons and the wheated whiskeys were bottled at 105 proof and 103 proof, respectively.
  • Bib & Tucker is launching its first bonded bourbon. The Tennessee-based distillery debuted an 8-year-old high-rye bottled at 100 proof. The bourbon’s nationwide rollout will begin September and come with a suggested retail price of $64.99.
  • Old Overholt debuted an 11-year-old Kentucky-style rye. The release marks the distillery’s fourth installment of its Extra Aged Cask Strength series. Old Overholt Extra Aged Cask Strength 11YR 2026 Edition is bottled at 125.6 proof and available for a suggested retail price of $109.99.

title: 7 Things You Should Know About Sun Cruiser, Boston Beer Company’s Other Hard Tea
summary:
When Boston Beer Company (BBC) debuted Sun Cruiser in 2024, it wasn’t the first canned hard tea to join the craft beer juggernaut’s portfolio. The company was actually one of the earliest in the game, launching Twisted Tea in 2001 — a trailblazer in the category that’s still beloved by its loyal fans today. So, what does this new hard tea add to BBC’s portfolio? Whereas Twisted Tea aimed to mimic Southern sweet tea, Sun Cruiser played into low-sugar marketing off the bat, looking to appeal to sporty and outdoorsy types.

The article 7 Things You Should Know About Sun Cruiser, Boston Beer Company’s Other Hard Tea appeared first on VinePair.
content:
When Boston Beer Company (BBC) debuted Sun Cruiser in 2024, it wasn’t the first canned hard tea to join the craft beer juggernaut’s portfolio. The company was actually one of the earliest in the game, launching Twisted Tea in 2001 — a trailblazer in the category that’s still beloved by its loyal fans today. So, what does this new hard tea add to BBC’s portfolio?

Whereas Twisted Tea aimed to mimic Southern sweet tea, Sun Cruiser played into low-sugar marketing off the bat, looking to appeal to sporty and outdoorsy types. And rather than the malt-based liquor used in Twisted Tea, Sun Cruiser cans are spiked with vodka.

Sun Cruisers are quite of the moment, especially as RTDs — particularly spiked teas and lemonades — continue to fly off of shelves. They also come in at just 4.5 percent ABV, a mark that has established itself as the norm in recent years. Plus, they are still a trendsetting feature as the industry moves to offer non-carbonated alternatives in the RTD space. From appealing flavors to strategic partnerships, here are seven things to know about Sun Cruiser, BBC’s “other” hard tea brand.

  1. Sun Cruiser has just four flavors, but more may be on the horizon.

    Beyond Classic Iced Tea, the brand offers a Half and Half (a mix of lemonade and iced tea), as well as peach and raspberry flavors — all of which were part of the product’s initial launch. Earlier this year, Sun Cruiser released an additional line of hard teas called White Tea + Vodka to select markets. The White Tea variety pack has its own suite of four flavors: berry hibiscus, blackberry, passionfruit, and peach.

  2. The brand expanded to include lemonade in 2025.

    Roughly a year after Sun Cruiser reached markets nationwide, the brand added a suite of lemonades to its portfolio. Its canned vodka and lemonade came at a time when several major companies launched similar products. Sun Cruiser debuted the secondary lineup with classic, 50/50, pink, and strawberry lemonade flavors. Now, the line also includes blueberry lemonade, which joined the Sun Cruiser portfolio earlier this year.

  3. Each can contains 100 calories and one gram of sugar.

    The first phrase to pop up on Sun Cruiser’s website and Instagram bio are, “Real Iced Tea. Real Vodka.” Its wellness ethos is one that feeds into much of its marketing materials. Across its site, Sun Cruiser advertises that each can contains only 100 calories and only 1 gram of sugar. (The bottom of each can does say “Made with tea, natural flavors, and artificial sweeteners, however).

  4. The company partners with golfwear and beachwear brands.

    Sun Cruiser announced collaborations with lifestyle brand Jetty and golf apparel brand G/Force in 2025 and 2026, respectively. The partnership with Jetty consists of beachware, including sun-protective hoodies, tank tops, and bucket hats. The line with G/Force is a suite of golf equipment branded with the hard tea company’s logo on pieces like polos and gloves.

  5. The brand was the official RTD of the 2026 U.S. Open golf tournament.

    Sun Cruiser dialed into its affiliation with sports with a partnership with the United States Golf Association, landing the spot as the official RTD of both the U.S. Open and U.S. Women’s Open in 2026. The partnership included a number of on-site stunts, including staged caddies dressed in branded bibs and golf carts exclusively selling Sun Cruiser products.

  6. Sun Cruiser loves interacting with fans online.

    Many posts on Sun Cruiser’s Instagram account are carousels featuring photos from fans candidly enjoying cans of the hard tea. The brand compiles them and attaches a caption to each one, such as “gone cruisin’” and “where you’ll find me this weekend.” Fans have submitted photos of themselves drinking cans of Sun Cruiser at Boston’s Fenway Park, at the beach, on a pontoon boat, and other adventurous locations.

  7. From keychains to ball markers, Sun Cruiser has its own line of merchandise.

    Beyond the partnered lines of merchandise, Sun Cruiser boasts its own lineup of branded lifestyle items. There’s golf equipment like a ball marker and a club towel, home-bartending products like a mat and a bottle opener, and apparel like a bandana. There’s also a 32-ounce bucket sporting the brand’s logo designed for “sunny days, tailgates, beach hangs, and backyard lounging,” according to the website.

title: Turning up the Heat: The Surge of Spicy Cocktails (Plus 3 Recipes to Try)
summary:
Jump to Tequila Zarpado REAPER cocktail recipes here! The din of curious conversation fills a neighborhood cocktail bar. Placed atop a coaster, a rocks glass is then delicately topped with a chili garnish. A bottle of amber-gold tequila with red peppers and the words “ZARPADO REAPER” emblazoned on the label can be spotted behind the bar. Across New York City, and increasingly across bars and homes throughout the country, cocktail enthusiasts are seeking unique experiences.

The article Turning up the Heat: The Surge of Spicy Cocktails (Plus 3 Recipes to Try) appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Jump to Tequila Zarpado REAPER cocktail recipes here!

The din of curious conversation fills a neighborhood cocktail bar. Placed atop a coaster, a rocks glass is then delicately topped with a chili garnish. A bottle of amber-gold tequila with red peppers and the words “ZARPADO REAPER” emblazoned on the label can be spotted behind the bar.

Across New York City, and increasingly across bars and homes throughout the country, cocktail enthusiasts are seeking unique experiences. The era of straightforward sweet and sour cocktails has passed, and bartenders are rewriting the rules to deliver a full spectrum of flavors that include savory as well as spicy.

Though the Bloody Mary and Spicy Margarita certainly whet the palate for spice in a cocktail, the movement has evolved beyond those staples, and proved to have the staying power needed to become a fixture in cocktail culture rather than a passing fad.

“Bartenders today are trying to build more layered, complex drinks,” says Evgeny Tolmachev, head bartender at Mace NYC, about the growth of the spicy cocktail category. “Guests don’t just ask for a Margarita anymore; they’ll say they want something spicy, bitter, or savory. Those flavor profiles have become a part of the conversation.”

Rather than relying on sweet, sour, or bitter, spice shifts a drink’s complexity with even more depth, especially when not every heat is the same. 

Chili liqueurs, pepper tinctures and spicy bitters are just a few ways to add heat to a drink. Bartenders in New York City are favoring infused spirits in place of muddling peppers to create a controllable, consistent level of spice, according to Ginn Choe, mixologist of Ligaw NYC and beverage manager of Club 3 on the TV series “Bobby’s Triple Threat.”

The flavor profile of tequila lends itself well to spice. The bright freshness and subtle herbal notes of the agave in tequila complement a pepper spice. Some peppers carry a fruity finish underneath all that heat, which further complements the characteristics of good tequila. 

All three of the bartenders whose talents contributed the drinks featured are fans of the Carolina Reaper-and Habanero-infused REAPER by Tequila Zarpado.

REAPER comes together using the brand’s small-batch blanco as a base, carrying traditional notes of Weber blue agave with the flavor characteristics of the pepper. Zarpado is the only tequila producer currently using the Carolina Reaper, famously the “world’s hottest pepper,” in this way, though the sensation is less about pure heat and more about the way the spice gives way to a fruitiness underneath. This structure gives bartenders room to build complex flavors in cocktails around the spirit.

At Mace, the West Village cocktail bar known for its global approach to herbs and spices, Tolmachev balances flavors and techniques while also operating a bartender education channel on YouTube. For his REAPER cocktail, a riff on the Picante de la Casa, he wanted to bring culinary elements to the mix while highlighting the tequila’s heat.

“It combines fresh herbs and pepper in a very natural way,” says Tolmachev. “It’s simple and memorable.”

His Picante de la Casa uses lime and agave to draw out the tequila’s fruit character, while swapping the original recipe’s cilantro for basil. This adds a fresh, approachable snap that tempers REAPER’s spice while still letting the heat shine. “A well-made pepper infusion or spirit makes recipe development much more reliable. It allows you to focus on balance instead of constantly adjusting for variations in the peppers,” Tolmachev says.

Meanwhile, Ginn Choe’s approach to her cocktail, the Spicy Paloma, uses the tequila’s heat to bring balance to the tequila and grapefruit ingredients, rather than reinventing it. Here, Zarpado’s REAPER is mixed with grapefruit and lime juices, agave syrup, and a topper of club soda, finished with a grapefruit twist.

Asked why the Paloma made sense as a base for a spicy riff, Choe says: “The tang of fine red grapefruit and citrus, and the sweet heat of the Reaper peppers come together into the drink. It’s a classic with a wonderful combination that pairs well with food to finalize a table by elevating any bite.”

To keep the citrus from getting lost against the spice, Choe added a touch of extra lime to bring out the Paloma’s characteristics while making it easy to make at home.

At Lucky Tiger NYC, head bartender Matt Almodiel took REAPER in a savory, corn-forward direction with the Cornography. He uses Nixta, a corn liqueur, as well as a sweet corn syrup to enhance the savory-yet-sweet flavor profile, while Kota Pandan liqueur adds body.

Served over ice in a rocks glass, the Cornography uses REAPER’s heat as an extension of the tequila’s earthier characteristics.

The three cocktails are unique and distinct, but all rely on highlighting different complexities found in a pepper-infused spicy spirit — proof that heat in a cocktail isn’t one-dimensional. The restrained Picante de la Casa, balanced Spicy Paloma and savory Cornography all use spice as a cocktail building block in the same way as sour or bitter. 

The versatility of this flavor element is why spicy cocktails have become a permanent part of cocktail culture. With social media helping push and shape global trends and palates, guests are more receptive than ever when it comes to choosing exciting new options on cocktail menus. 

The next wave of NYC’s most interesting cocktails may not come from unearthing a forgotten classic or inventing a new technique, but from finding new ways to play with complex flavors like spice, while keeping them the main character of the drink.

So the next time your drink comes with a chile garnish, don’t shy away from the heat — embrace it, and see where those flavors take you.

Recipes

Picante de la Casa

Ingredients

  • 2 ounces Zarpado REAPER Tequila
  • 3/4 ounce fresh lime juice
  • 1/4 ounce agave nectar
  • 1 lime wedge
  • A few basil leaves

Directions

  1. In a cocktail shaker, shake all ingredients with ice.
  2. Fine strain into a rocks glass.
  3. Garnish with fresh basil.

Spicy Paloma

Ingredients

  • 1 1/2 ounces Zarpado REAPER Tequila
  • 1 1/2 ounces grapefruit juice
  • 1/2 ounce lime juice
  • 3/4 ounce agave syrup

Directions

  1. In a cocktail shaker, shake all ingredients with ice.
  2. Strain into *glass over ice.
  3. Top with club soda.
  4. Garnish with a grapefruit twist.

*Glassware: Palomas are typically served in a highball glass, but feel free to style like Ginn in a fun wine glass!

Cornography

Ingredients

  • 1 1/4 ounces Zarpado REAPER Tequila
  • 1/2 ounce Nixta
  • 1/2 ounce Kota Pandan
  • 1/2 ounce sweet corn syrup 
  • 1/2 ounce lime
  • 1/4 ounce sour cream whey
  • 2 dashes orange bitters 

Directions

  1. In a cocktail shaker, shake all ingredients with ice.
  2. Double strain.
  3. Garnish with corn.

This article is sponsored by Tequila Zarpado.

title: India Pale Ale Is Still Synonymous With Craft Beer, and That’s a Problem
summary:
In 2014, I published a throwaway listicle at Thrillist about India Pale Ales. Specifically, why I hated them: Why can’t I just enjoy it? Why does every single IPA make my gut bubble like a Jacuzzi full of soup? Every cicerone is my mortal enemy, every bar with rotating taps, my hop-hell. Oh, you disagree? Pound sand/shred me in the comments, because the reasons for my IPA hatred are completely unassailable. You get the idea. This piece, basically just a grievance blog I threw together in my spare time, went pretty viral when it was published a dozen years ago.

The article India Pale Ale Is Still Synonymous With Craft Beer, and That’s a Problem appeared first on VinePair.
content:
In 2014, I published a throwaway listicle at Thrillist about India Pale Ales. Specifically, why I hated them:

Why can’t I just enjoy it? Why does every single IPA make my gut bubble like a Jacuzzi full of soup? Every cicerone is my mortal enemy, every bar with rotating taps, my hop-hell. Oh, you disagree? Pound sand/shred me in the comments, because the reasons for my IPA hatred are completely unassailable.

You get the idea. This piece, basically just a grievance blog I threw together in my spare time, went pretty viral when it was published a dozen years ago. This was an odd moment in media, when legacy outlets still hadn’t gotten the hang of the digital commons and upstart publications could corner gobs of traffic with low-calorie takes calibrated to troll schlubs on Facebook. That era of the media business is emphatically gone, and that’s probably for the best. But in a somewhat shocking turn of events, the era of IPAs is still very much in force in the craft-brewing business, and all personal gripes aside, that is not for the best.

Earlier this month, the Brewers Association (BA) released its annual midyear report on the state of the segment. It’s the mixed bag you’ve come to expect if you’ve been tracking craft beer’s performance since the pandemic: Volume is down 4 percent year over year through the first six months of the year, but some 54 percent of respondents to the org’s survey are reporting growth. (The BA’s data-gathering operation is plenty fallible, as we learned earlier this year, so, y’know, grain of salt and all that. But it is still the best publicly available reporting on the segment, and furnishes an important directional marker.) It is good that more than half of the breweries responding to the BA are seeing growth; that figure stood at 49 percent last year. “While the findings point to continued pressure, several indicators suggest the contraction may be moderating,” wrote Matt Gacioch, the BA’s staff economist. Maybe!

There’s less mystery in trying to tease out what is driving the growth, especially at scale, and especially-especially in the package. It’s IPAs, man. As Beer Marketer’s Insights first noted last week, of the top 30 craft brands selling in multi-outlet grocery, mass retail, and convenience stores tracked by the market research firm Circana through July 12, only 11 of them are in the black year to date by dollars. All 11 are IPAs. In order of descending volume, they are:

  • Voodoo Ranger Imperial (up 7.3 percent in dollars and 5.3 percent in cases)
  • Voodoo Ranger Juice Force (+10.6 and +8.7 percent)
  • Sierra Nevada Hazy Little Thing (+8.3 and +6.4 percent)
  • Elysian Space Dust (+11.3 and +9.7 percent)
  • Lagunitas India Pale Ale (+2.1 and +1.4 percent)
  • Goose Island Tropical Beer Hug (+4.3 and +1.2 percent)
  • Cigar City Jai Alai (+6.5 and +2.5 percent)
  • Lagunitas A Little Sumpin’ Sumpin’ (+18.5 and +18.3 percent)
  • Wicked Weed Pernicious (+11.7 and +11.7 percent)
  • Georgetown Bodhizafa (+13.6 and +13.1 percent)
  • Voodoo Ranger G-Force Supercharged (which is already the 24th best-selling craft beer in the Circana-verse despite only being launched in February of this year.)

Two more beers are less than 1 percent in the red in YTD dollars: They are also IPAs.

“[C]raft sales remain a tale of IPAs vs all other in off-prem scans,” wrote BMI. No kidding.

There are caveats. The off-premise is not the total market, and craft beer has traditionally overindexed in both the on-premise generally and draft specifically. “Whereas beer overall has sold less than 50% draft by volume each year since 2017, craft has hovered around 80% draft at bars over the past decade,” the BA’s Gacioch wrote in a May 2026 blog post assessing on-premise trends. Non-IPA styles typically have a much better shot over the bar, particularly in a pint glass. (When was the last time you saw a 19.2-ounce stovepipe of pilsner in the convenience-store fridge? Exactly.) There’s some evidence that styles other than IPA are breaking through over the bar.

For example, of the top five styles by share tracked by the on-premise analytics platform BeerBoard, only “lager” and “wheat/hefeweisen” gained draft share during the four-week period from June 11-28, when the World Cup action was new/novel and hot/heavy. Craft brewers enjoyed some of that share growth. Still, the overall segment was down around 2 percent share by volume and 2.5 percent share by dollars, in no small part because IPA lost a share point in this slice of BeerBoard data. On-premise or off-premise, as goes IPA, so goes craft.

I don’t really hate IPAs all that much anymore. I don’t drink them that often, but I don’t have a problem with them. But I really think the craft-brewing industry does. Remember how that hack last year wrote that lazy op-ed for The New York Times titled “Wacky Names and Silly Labels Are Killing Craft Beer”? And we all made fun of it because it sucked and was stupid? Good fun, that. But as I wrote at the time, “There are some good observations buried among this bleating, even if they’re obvious to industry insiders and intuitive to all but the most casual drinkers.” One of those kernels of truth is that IPAs — on which around half of all off-premise dollars are spent, per Circana — cannot continue to sustain this segment on their own.

It’s not just me, a known hater, saying this. The BA’s chief executive and president, Bart Watson, has been sounding that alarm for years. At the trade group’s annual Craft Brewers Conference in 2024, for example, he warned of a day when IPA may no longer stand for “Immediate Profits Ahead.” The Gray Lady’s anti-IPA rant was dumb and bad because it misunderstood cause and effect: “Brewers don’t make IPAs because they’re “obsess[ed]” with them, they make them because that’s what sells,” I wrote. They were selling way back in 2014, when I first outed myself as an IPA antagonist, and they are still selling now, as the latest scan data indicate. But the competition is a lot stiffer for fridge space than it was a dozen years ago. The American drinking public is no longer dazzled by the novelty of heavily hopped West Coast IPAs or even juicy New England IPAs. There are BuzzBallz to be guzzled and Surfsides to be slugged. The most stupid-simple, flavor-forward style craft beer had to offer is complicated in comparison with its competition.

This lengthy IPA reign is starting to feel like the end of history for the segment. Nearly a decade since the introduction of Voodoo Ranger and more than half a dozen years since the summer of White Claw, it has found no heir apparent. This is the real danger. It’s not that sales of the style might suddenly collapse, vaporizing half the segment’s revenue and dragging innumerable breweries under. It’s not that dimwits with pals at legacy media outlets occasionally whine about the style in poorly reasoned op-eds. It’s that the entire segment is stuck on IPAs, and couldn’t move past them even if it wanted to. It’s a hoppy hostage situation, basically. This is an odd moment in the craft-brewing business, and it’s been going on for quite some time.

🤯 Hop-ocalypse Now

It is of course well understood that Boston Beer Company is a “beer company” in name only, but its most recent earnings report really drove the point home. Of all the legacy craft brewery’s brands, not a single malt-based one was in the black for the second quarter of the year — not even Dogfish Head, which had been on a bit of a run thanks to the outsized (and frankly surprising) success of its Grateful Dead collaboration. Overall, depletions were down 6 percent for the quarter, despite growth from Angry Orchard and Sun Cruiser. Will BBC’s new vodka sports drink, Rally Dog, start another spirits-based rally?

📈 Ups…

Independent Michelob Ultra challenger Hero95 doubled its volume year-over-year on the back of a crazy conversion rate for sampling… Tilray Brands lost $105.2 million last year, which sounds bad until you remember it lost $2.2 billion the year before last… Samuel Adams is rolling out an apple-spice ale for fall, finally…

📉 …and downs

The liberal activist/brewery operator behind Minocqua Brewing Company announced Wisconsin officials are preparing to revoke the firm’s permit in an act of “heavy-handed” tax enforcement… New Associated Press analysis shows grocery prices have risen an astonishing 33 percent since 2019, its biggest seven-year leap in half a century… Anheuser-Busch InBev posted small declines in Q2 depletions and shipments in the U.S., even as Cutwater kept soaring…

The article Jameson Announces Partnership With the NFL, Replacing Diageo As Official Spirits Sponsor appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Jameson Irish Whiskey will replace Diageo as the official spirits sponsor for the National Football League (NFL). On Thursday, Jameson announced that parent company Pernod Ricard inked a multiyear deal with the NFL, handing exclusive marketing rights at certain national and international matches to the Irish whiskey category leader.

According to a report in Sports Business Journal, Pernod Ricard’s partnership is worth approximately $20 million each year. The announcement comes a few months after Diageo’s decision to forgo renewing its five-year, cross-portfolio contract with the league in April. Diageo, owner of brands like Bailey’s, Crown Royal, Johnnie Walker, Smirnoff, and Tanqueray, became the NFL’s first official spirits sponsor in 2021.

The new contract will see Jameson as the leading sponsor of the Super Bowl Tailgate Concert and four of the league’s international games this year. The brand will also install branded pop-up bars at the NFL Draft, Super Bowl Experience fan festival, and other marquee moments in the upcoming season.

“Football is a sport driven by passion, ritual, and unforgettable community connections — values that lie at the very heart of Jameson,” Colin Kavanagh, chief marketing officer of Pernod Ricard North America said in a release. The Paris-based company, also behind brands like Absolut, Beefeater, and The Glenlivet, is optimistic about the opportunity for Jameson to reach more fans as the NFL expands on a global level.

Jameson will join Anheuser-Busch InBev’s Bud Light and Gallo’s Barefoot, the official beer and wine of the league, as the spirits sponsor for the NFL. Jameson is also the official whiskey of Major League Soccer.

Will American football fans take to the new spirit? We’ll have to see if Jamo shots become the new tailgate and touchdown ritual.

title: 9 Bartenders Share Their Favorite Frozen Cocktail to Make at Home
summary:
There’s no need to relegate frozen drinks to just one season, but a frosty beverage does hit different in the summer. When temperatures touch the triple digits, walking into a bar and simply seeing a churning frozen machine perched on the counter can feel just as refreshing as taking a sip. Even if you decide to host at home instead of going out, it doesn’t mean you have to give up your frozen Piña Coladas or icy Miami Vices.

The article 9 Bartenders Share Their Favorite Frozen Cocktail to Make at Home appeared first on VinePair.
content:
There’s no need to relegate frozen drinks to just one season, but a frosty beverage does hit different in the summer. When temperatures touch the triple digits, walking into a bar and simply seeing a churning frozen machine perched on the counter can feel just as refreshing as taking a sip.

Even if you decide to host at home instead of going out, it doesn’t mean you have to give up your frozen Piña Coladas or icy Miami Vices. Most frozen cocktails come together easily in a blender and are simple to batch for a crowd, making them the perfect party drink.

So we tapped bartenders from across the country to find out which frozen drinks they make when they’re off the clock. From quintessential picks to cocktails like Espresso Martinis and Garibaldis turned frosty, here’s how nine top bartenders make frozen drinks at home for summertime soirées and beyond.

Izler Thomas

Bar manager and head mixologist, Tiya, San Francisco

For me, this is the perfect at-home frozen cocktail because it feels familiar and nostalgic. It has everything I love about an Espresso Martini: the rich coffee flavor and gentle kick but with the creamy texture of a frozen café drink. Imagine sitting outside on a bright sunny afternoon with an ice-cold coffee in your hand, except it’s actually a cocktail. That’s exactly the experience I wanted to create.

Ingredients

  • 1½ ounces vodka
  • 1½ ounces fresh espresso (or 1 teaspoon instant coffee dissolved in a splash of hot water)
  • 2 generous scoops pistachio ice cream
  • Ice

Directions

  1. Add the vodka, espresso, pistachio ice cream, and a handful of ice to a blender.
  2. Blend until thick, smooth, and frozen with a milkshake-like consistency.
  3. Taste and adjust with a little more ice if you’d like it thicker.
  4. Pour into a coffee mug or chilled coupe and enjoy immediately.

Ana Jovic

Beverage director, Lucky Cheetah, Portland, Maine

My favorite frozen drink to make at home is basically the Negroni’s fun, approachable cousin. It’s the easiest “impressive” drink in my back pocket — only two ingredients, no fancy equipment, and the bitter-sweet Campari against the sweet OJ just works in frozen form. Also it’s basically neon orange, so it’s an instant mood on a hot day.

Ingredients

  • 4 to 5 ounces fresh orange juice
  • 1 ½ ounces Campari
  • 1 ½ cups ice
  • Garnish: orange wheel or twist

Directions

  1. Combine Campari, orange juice, and ice in a blender.
  2. Blend until smooth and slushy, about 20 to 30 seconds.
  3. Pour into a wine glass or large rocks glass.
  4. Garnish with an orange wheel or twist.

Mariena Mercer Boarini

Master mixologist, Wynn Resorts North America, Las Vegas

If I’m making a frozen cocktail at home, I almost always reach for a frozen Hugo Spritz. It feels like summer in a glass — bright, floral, and incredibly refreshing — but it’s also one of the easiest frozen cocktails to make. Because it relies on just three ingredients, there’s very little prep, and the elderflower and mint create an elegant flavor profile that tastes far more complex than the recipe suggests. It’s the kind of drink I make when friends stop by unexpectedly or when we’re spending an afternoon outside. I also really adore frozen carbonated elements for a pop of surprise and delight.

Ingredients

  • 3 ounces Prosecco
  • 1 ½ ounces St-Germain elderflower liqueur
  • 1 ounce soda water
  • 1 ½ cups pebble or crushed ice
  • Garnish: mint

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a blender with ice. Blend until smooth.
  2. Pour into a wine glass and garnish with fresh mint.

Justin Ware

Beverage director, Johnny’s Gold Brick, Starduster, and Winnie’s, Houston

I don’t make a lot of frozen drinks at home, but if I’m busting out the Vitamix I want to get textures that can only be achieved in a blender rather than the frozen machines at work. The greatest example of this is the El Floridita Daiquiri. Invented in Havana in the early 20th century, I think it’s the first-known blender drink and still the best. My favorite version is the recipe given to me by my buddy, former co-worker, and current Portland, Maine, bar owner (shoutout Cuties), Garrett Lenderman. The key to this version is to use granulated sugar and do not overblend; you want a crunchy, slightly gritty slushie texture that you can’t get in a frozen machine.

Ingredients

  • 2 ounces white rum (Probitas or Plantation 3 Stars)
  • 1 ¼ ounces fresh lime juice
  • 2 tablespoons granulated sugar
  • ¼ ounce Luxardo Maraschino
  • 12 ounces crushed ice
  • Garnish: Maraschino cherry and lime wheel

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a Vitamix or other high-powered blender.
  2. Blend on high for 7 to 10 seconds, until you stop hearing individual pieces of ice crack and consistency is that of a thick slurpee. It should require a spoon or some jiggling of the blender if done properly.
  3. Pour into a coupe glass. Garnish with a maraschino cherry and lime wheel.

Kevin Beary

Beverage director, Gus’ Sip & Dip, Kitty’s Cosmopolitan Club, and Three Dots and a Dash, Chicago

I am a stan for a Hemingway Daiquiri. But to make this well, it requires more work than your average home cook may be interested in. I can try to simplify it, but I promise it’s worth the extra work.

Ingredients

  • 8 ounces Real McCoy 3 Barbados Rum
  • 5 ounces grapefruit juice
  • 2 ounces grapefruit super oleo saccharum (or other grapefruit syrup)
  • 1 ounce Maraschino liqueur
  • Full sized ice cubes to fill blender
  • Garnish: grapefruit zest

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a blender and fill with full-size ice cubes (not crushed ice) to the 48-ounce line on your blender canister.
  2. Blend on high until smooth. If you nailed the ice-to-cocktail ratio this should be nice and thick and stack in the glass as you pour it.
  3. Pour into a fizz or deep coupe glass. Use a microplane to grate some fresh grapefruit zest over the top.

Jacob Coombs

Owner and head bartender, The Marquis Lounge, Portland, Maine

I love this Cachaça limonada because it reminds me of mixing lime into coconuts on the beach bar I worked at in St. Croix. A beautiful blend using the crushability and bitterness of a Brazilian lemonade, the simplicity of a Caipirinha, and the grassiness of Wray and Nephew with a touch of bison grass.

Ingredients

  • 3 ounces Brazilian lemonade
  • 1 ounce Cachaça
  • ½ ounce Wray & Nephew White Overproof Rum
  • ½ ounce Zubrowka Bison Grass Vodka
  • ¾ ounce pure cane syrup
  • Ice to preference

Directions

  1. Make Brazilian lemonade by blending three cups of water with three frozen limes cut into quarters.
  2. Add all additional ingredients to the blender with ice. Blend until smooth.
  3. Pour into a highball glass.

Ahu Hettema

Owner, Istanbul Hawaii, Honolulu

My favorite frozen drink to make at home is a frozen limonana with dates and cardamom. It is bright, cooling, and familiar, but the date syrup adds depth while the cardamom gives it a distinctly Turkish warmth.

Ingredients

  • 2 ounces gin or vodka
  • 1 ounce fresh lemon juice
  • ¾ ounce date syrup
  • 2 green cardamom pods, seeds removed and lightly crushed
  • 1½ cups ice
  • Pinch of sea salt
  • Garnish: mint leaves

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a blender and blend until smooth.
  2. Pour into a highball glass. Garnish with fresh mint.

Adam Griggs

Bar director, Amasa, New York City

I love making big batches of frozen Margaritas at home, and I developed this recipe so that I can make a big batch of drinks quickly and get a round out to everyone at the party without sacrificing quality. To achieve this, I build my batch in a blender, adding just enough ice to chill the drink and add the appropriate amount of dilution without turning it into a slushie. I like to start with a pretty standard Margarita ratio but depending on what spirits I have on hand, I often split the base between mezcal and tequila.

Ingredients

  • 2 parts tequila or mezcal (or half and half)
  • 1 part triple sec
  • 1 part lime juice
  • ½ part ice
  • ¼ part agave syrup
  • Garnish: lime wheel

Directions

  1. Combine all ingredients including ice in a blender and blend until smooth.
  2. Pour into salt-rimmed glasses over fresh ice.
  3. Garnish with a lime wheel.

Watermelon is one of my favorite frozen cocktail ingredients. It’s fresh, the color is striking, and its high water content makes for a smooth blend. This cocktail is easy to make at home and comes together in just a few minutes, which is exactly what I want from a frozen drink on a hot day.

Ingredients

  • 3 ounces watermelon juice
  • 1 ½ ounces simple syrup
  • 1 ¾ ounces St. George Green Chile Vodka
  • Ice to preference

Directions

  1. Add all ingredients to a blender with ice.
  2. Pour into a large rocks glass. Serve with a fresh squeeze of lime.
